status_reason: Provisional: both streams and the target variables (protein, fat) are stated, but concentration ranges, sampling points and the accuracy target are missing.
answer: Test NIR on both streams, but with separate interfaces: transmission or transflection for the clear whey and diffuse reflection for the opaque concentrate, each with its own calibration against independent laboratory protein and fat results. Transmission fails when milk is thick or fat-rich, and reflection is less representative for clear liquids, so one shared interface is only a hypothesis. If NIR misses the accuracy target, compare MIR ATR as a second method.

inline.headline: Test NIR transmission/transflection on the whey stream and NIR diffuse reflection on the concentrate, each with its own calibration.
inline.probe: NIR transmission/transflection probe with a controlled 1-10 mm path for whey; NIR diffuse reflection probe for the concentrate
inline.install: whey: in the clear stream line at a controlled path; concentrate: flush-mounted in the pipe or vat
inline.test_against: NIR diffuse reflection on the whey stream and NIR transmission on the concentrate, to compare the interfaces on each stream
inline.not_final_because: No spectra or accuracy data are supplied, so NIR is a hypothesis until its models meet the client's protein and fat target on held-out samples for each stream. Transmission cannot penetrate thick or fat-rich milk. The silica fiber range ends at 2400 nm while NIR is listed to 2500 nm, so the upper edge must be checked.

problems.text: The clear whey and the opaque concentrate need different optical interfaces and separate calibrations. One shared interface is only a hypothesis to test, although one NIR spectrometer can serve both interface types.
A transmission probe on the opaque concentrate will not work, because light cannot penetrate milk that is too thick or fat-rich.
A reflection probe is the wrong default for the clear whey, because reflection can be less representative for clear liquids.
NIR alone is assumed to be sufficient. Its bands are broad and overlapping and need chemometric models, and other methods can add molecular specificity that NIR may miss in dairy.

methods.why: Suits the clear whey stream, where the path length must be controlled at 1-10 mm, and a transflection probe may cover both low-fat and high-fat products.
Suits the opaque concentrate when the probe is flush-mounted in the pipe or vat; it is sensitive to fat globule size.
Has well-defined absorption peaks and high selectivity, with a 1-6 micrometre sampling depth on liquids and soft pastes, and can add specificity that NIR might miss.
Is complementary to MIR but needs special probes, and fluorescence can mask the signal for many organic compounds.

questions.q: What are the protein and fat ranges in the whey stream and in the concentrate?
questions.why: These set the path length, and transmission needs a controlled 1-10 mm path that fails on thick or fat-rich product.

questions.q: What is the pipe or vessel geometry and the sampling point for each stream, including flow, temperature and whether a bypass is possible?
questions.why: A flush-mounted reflection probe needs access to the pipe or vat, and the whey needs a defined path.

questions.q: How many paired laboratory protein and fat results can you collect for each stream, and what is the laboratory method and its precision?
questions.why: Models must be built and validated on independent laboratory references before they are applied.

questions.q: Is the whey ever cloudy or fouled, and does the concentrate vary in fat globule size or homogenisation?
questions.why: Clarity decides whether transmission stays valid, and reflection is sensitive to fat globule size.

experiment.objective: Compare NIR transmission/transflection and NIR diffuse reflection on each stream against laboratory protein and fat results, with one calibration per stream and interface.
steps: Collect paired samples from each stream across its operating range, with laboratory protein and fat as independent reference values.
Measure every stream with both NIR interfaces, recording the path length for each measurement.
Apply MSC or SNV scatter correction before PLS and build one calibration per stream and per interface.
Validate each model on held-out samples, and keep one shared interface only if a single model meets the accuracy target on both streams.
If NIR misses the target, run MIR ATR on a subset of the same samples as the comparison, and keep a combination only if it beats the best single method on the same validation data.
references: S01 p.17 (inline milk analysis; MSC/SNV before PLS for fat and protein)
S01 p.18 (transmission versus reflection in dairy)
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client: the accuracy target for protein and fat per stream, to be set before the trial.

pathway.key_features: No spectra are supplied, so the key features must be identified in the lab trial; fat and protein bands are listed at 0.85-1.1 micrometres in the band chart.
pathway.path_reason: Key spectral features must be identified in the lab trial before a solution is chosen.

multispectral.why: MIR gives well-defined absorption peaks where NIR bands overlap, so it may add molecular specificity that NIR misses in dairy.
multispectral.test: Compare the NIR-only model with the NIR + MIR ATR model on the same validation samples for each stream, and keep the combination only if it beats the best single method. Switch to a combined same-spot probe if the spectra differ by sampling spot.

assumptions: Protein and fat are the only target variables for the pilot.
One NIR spectrometer can serve both interfaces, as reported for dairy, but this is not yet verified for these streams.
Paired laboratory results can be collected for both streams.
Stream temperature, fat globule size and concentration range are not stated and are assumed to vary within the operating range.
